headline: Ecopetrol: profit up 86% on record refining margins and higher oil prices, with Brazil’s Brava Energia added in September
takeaway: Net income rose 86% to COP 4.8 trillion (about US$1.45 billion, or roughly US$0.70 per ADS) on revenue up 18% to COP 35.1 trillion, driven by higher crude prices and a record refining margin. The quarter included the first month of Brava Energia, the Brazilian producer Ecopetrol bought 51% of for US$1.12 billion.
results: Ecopetrol reported net income attributable to shareholders of about COP 4.8 trillion for the third quarter, up 85.6% from COP 2.6 trillion a year earlier, on revenue of COP 35.1 trillion, up 18%, and EBITDA of COP 15.9 trillion, according to its results release and press reports. At the November 13 exchange rate that is roughly US$1.45 billion, or about US$0.70 per ADS.

For the first nine months revenue rose 14.3% to COP 103.9 trillion, EBITDA 28% to COP 47.0 trillion and net income 83% to COP 13.7 trillion, even though sales volumes fell 2.7%. Income tax expense doubled to COP 9.9 trillion, lifting the effective rate to 37.3% from 32.1%. Refining margins reached a record of about US$45.6 a barrel.

Ecopetrol completed the purchase of 51% of Brava Energia on August 17 for US$1.123 billion. Brava contributed COP 1.1 trillion of revenue and COP 0.6 trillion of EBITDA in September, and added COP 27.5 trillion of assets. Group production averaged about 747,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day.
mgmt: Management said results were in line with its announced ranges and kept its 2026 net income guidance of COP 12–16 trillion, which the nine-month result already sits within. It emphasised stronger free cash flow, sustainable debt, cost discipline and competitive shareholder returns.
Press coverage noted that, excluding Brava, output declined, debt rose and the company has changed management during the year, while exchange-rate movements weighed on reported results.
view: Ecopetrol is a reminder that integrated oil companies earn money in more than one place. This quarter the refineries did the heavy lifting: a record margin of around US$45 a barrel at Cartagena and Barrancabermeja, on top of higher crude prices, nearly doubled profit even as Colombian production slipped. Refining margins of that size reflect tight global diesel markets and are unlikely to last, which management’s own guidance range implicitly acknowledges.

The Brava deal is the strategic headline. Colombia stopped awarding new oil and gas exploration contracts under former President Gustavo Petro, which left Ecopetrol with declining domestic reserves. Buying control of a Brazilian producer is a way to replace them abroad, but it adds debt, currency exposure and integration risk to a company already carrying a heavy balance sheet, much of it from the earlier purchase of the power-transmission company ISA.

Ecopetrol trades at a low multiple and has historically paid high dividends because the Colombian state, its 88% owner, relies on the payouts. That makes the dividend both the attraction and the risk: if oil prices fall or refining margins normalise, the government’s need for cash could crowd out investment or force more borrowing. With a new government in office since August, energy policy — especially whether exploration licensing resumes — matters more to the long-term value than any single quarter.
watch: Watch refining margins in the fourth quarter, Brava’s integration and production, debt levels after the acquisition, the 2026 dividend proposal, and the new government’s energy policy.
